allObjections.title: Unbounded jsonb array growth
allObjections.detail: §2.1 delta_log[] and governance_record[] are append-only jsonb arrays with no retention policy or archival mechanism. A product with 365 daily runs accumulates thousands of entries, degrading query performance and making the 'one row per product+environment' design a liability.

allObjections.title: Hash chain verification gap
allObjections.detail: §3.1 computes this_hash during write but §8 criterion #6 only verifies nightly. A corrupted hash chain could persist for up to 24 hours before detection, and the spec provides no remediation path when divergence is found.

allObjections.title: Concurrent write serialization failure
allObjections.detail: §8 criterion #3 acknowledges concurrent writes may abort with serialization_failure but provides no retry logic or queue mechanism. High-traffic products could see frequent write failures during peak Self-Renewal hours.

allObjections.title: Override revocation creates infinite loops
allObjections.detail: §9 Q4 Option Y's 'revoke = new override with replacementContent' means revoking a revocation creates a third override. There's no mechanism to prevent oscillating override chains or to determine the 'true' original value after multiple revocations.

allObjections.title: Atomicity interpretation issues
allObjections.detail: The proposal uses a saga pattern for atomicity (§3.2), which may lead to inconsistencies if compensating actions fail. This could result in partial updates that are difficult to reconcile, especially if external systems like Vercel fail after the database transaction commits.

allObjections.title: RLS policy complexity
allObjections.detail: The split into three explicit per-role policies (§4.6) increases complexity and potential for misconfiguration. This could lead to unauthorized access or denial of access to legitimate users, impacting data security and usability.

allObjections.title: Cost implications of re-assessment crawl
allObjections.detail: The re-assessment crawl adds significant cost per Self-Renewal cycle (§7.1), which could become prohibitive as the number of products and environments scales. This might deter adoption or lead to budget overruns.

allObjections.title: Lack of rollback
allObjections.detail: The proposal does not provide a clear rollback strategy in case of failures during the atomic write transaction, which could lead to data inconsistencies and errors. Specifically, §3.1 does not specify how to handle failures during the transaction.

allObjections.title: Insufficient RLS
allObjections.detail: The RLS policies defined in §4.6 may not be sufficient to prevent unauthorized access to the ProductSSOT data, as they rely on the `auth.jwt()` function which may be vulnerable to tampering or spoofing. Additionally, the policies do not account for potential conflicts between different roles or users.

allObjections.title: Inadequate testing
allObjections.detail: The acceptance criteria defined in §8 may not be comprehensive enough to ensure the correct functioning of the ProductSSOT system, as they do not cover all possible scenarios or edge cases. For example, the criteria do not test the behavior of the system in case of concurrent updates or failures during the atomic write transaction.

allObjections.title: Complexity in Self-Governance
allObjections.detail: The Self-Governance Layer introduces multiple components that need to interact seamlessly. The Self-Test component, for instance, requires a scheduledSelfTest that might conflict with other scheduled tasks, leading to resource contention. The Self-Audit component's five-dimension scoring engine adds complexity, especially with the introduction of the Security Posture dimension, which could lead to false positives and unnecessary Self-Protection triggers.

allObjections.title: Risk of Self-Protection Rollback
allObjections.detail: The Self-Protect component's snapshot and rollback mechanism before any state mutation is critical but risky. If the rollback mechanism fails or is improperly triggered, it could lead to data loss or inconsistent states. The proposal does not detail the failure recovery process for the rollback mechanism.

allObjections.title: Human Gates Bottleneck
allObjections.detail: The four Human Gates introduce potential bottlenecks in the system. The Approval gate, for instance, requires elevated roles for overrides, which could delay critical decisions. The Testing gate's re-fix and escalate options add complexity and potential delays in the approval process.

allObjections.title: Complexity of Append-Only
allObjections.detail: The append-only model for overrides (§3 + §13.1) adds complexity to the system, as it requires maintaining a full history of changes, which can lead to performance issues and increased storage requirements over time.

allObjections.title: UI Friendliness
allObjections.detail: The append-only model may not be as user-friendly as the UPDATE-with-revision model, as it does not provide a consolidated view of an override's history, potentially leading to confusion for operators.

allObjections.title: RLS Policy Complexity
allObjections.detail: The append-only model may complicate the implementation of RLS policies, as it requires handling each override as a separate entry, which could lead to more complex policy definitions and potential security risks.

allObjections.title: RLS complexity
allObjections.detail: The RLS policies in §4.6, while seemingly straightforward, introduce significant complexity. The OR-combined policies, while semantically equivalent to the prior single policy, are harder to reason about and debug. Misconfiguration could lead to unintended data access or denial of service.

allObjections.title: Saga pattern risks
allObjections.detail: The saga pattern in §3.2, while pragmatic, introduces potential inconsistencies. If the post-commit side effects (Stage C) fail, the system logs the error but doesn't roll back the transaction. This could lead to a state where the ProductSSOT is updated, but the operator isn't notified or the UI isn't updated, leading to confusion and potential errors.

allObjections.title: Cost estimation uncertainty
allObjections.detail: The cost estimation in §7.1 for the re-assessment crawl is highly variable (~$0.30 – $2.00). This wide range makes it difficult to accurately budget for the feature and could lead to unexpected cost overruns if the actual cost trends towards the higher end of the estimate. The reliance on external services like Browserless and Anthropic introduces further uncertainty.

allObjections.title: Version monotonicity enforcement
allObjections.detail: §3.3 states that version monotonicity is enforced by the write contract, not by SQL. This relies on application-level logic to prevent race conditions and ensure correct versioning. While the acceptance criteria include a test for this, relying on application logic instead of database constraints increases the risk of data corruption or inconsistencies.

allObjections.title: Saga leaves unverified deployments
allObjections.detail: §3.2's saga pattern risks leaving live deployments in 'unverified' states if SSOT writes fail. This violates §7's output contract atomicity principle, as users could interact with functionally deployed but unrecorded products. The lack of auto-undeploy creates security drift where ProductSSOT diverges from reality.

allObjections.title: RLS policy bypass risk
allObjections.detail: §3.4 service-role writes bypass RLS without org-scoped validation. A compromised service role could inject cross-org data into any ProductSSOT row. The absence of product-org linkage checks during writes contradicts §4.6's read isolation guarantees.

allObjections.title: Unbounded override accumulation
allObjections.detail: §4.4's append-only overrides lack expiry mechanisms. Indefinite overrides in governance_record could mask recurring issues (e.g., suppressed security scores), violating §10.2's reconciliation principle where issues must be resolved, not perpetually overridden.

allObjections.title: Cost scaling blindspot
allObjections.detail: §7.1's $0.30-$2.00/run cost assumes static product volume. At 50 products with daily cycles, annual costs hit $11k-$73k with no dynamic throttling (e.g., cadence adjustment for low-priority products). This violates §7.6's cost governance intent.

allObjections.title: Append-only is underspecified
allObjections.detail: §9 Q4 is still explicitly marked OPEN, but §3 and §13.1 act as if append-only is already canonical. That creates a governance mismatch: implementers are told not to build revoke/revision UI until Q4 lands, yet the core write contract and data model already bake in one interpretation without settling the unresolved semantic question.

allObjections.title: Version rows conflate concerns
allObjections.detail: §2.2 `product_ssot_version` stores both immutable snapshots and operational metadata like `write_kind`, `written_by`, and the derived hash chain. That mixes audit, provenance, and state capture into one artifact, which makes later correction or replay logic brittle if the canonical meaning of an override changes or if a write is partially synthesized from multiple sources.

allObjections.title: RLS and admin overrides conflict
allObjections.detail: §4.4 says admin annotations + overrides must be honoured as CEO-equivalent directives, but §3.4 and §4.6 separately restrict direct table writes and rely on server-side functions. The proposal never defines whether an operator-visible override is read-time interpretation, write-time mutation, or both, so different services can easily diverge on whether an override is active.

allObjections.title: Append-only override semantics may lead to unbounded growth
allObjections.detail: §3 and §13.1 specify append-only semantics for overrides, which could result in unbounded growth in the `overrides[]` jsonb array. This may impact performance and storage requirements.

allObjections.title: Lack of explicit override revocation mechanism
allObjections.detail: The proposal relies on appending a new override entry to 'revoke' an existing one (§9 Q4). This may lead to confusion and potential inconsistencies if not properly handled by the UI and downstream consumers.

allObjections.title: RLS policies may not be robust against concurrent writes
allObjections.detail: §4.6 defines RLS policies for `product_ssot`, but there is a risk of concurrent writes causing inconsistencies or policy violations if not properly synchronized.

allObjections.title: §3.2 saga omits external failure compensation
allObjections.detail: The three-stage saga table in §3.2 defines compensating actions only for Postgres txn failure (mark unverified) but provides no handler for Vercel deploy succeeding while delta report file write fails; this leaves the run in a half-cleared state where ClearanceRecord Step 6 can still pass despite missing §7 item #3 source disclosure.

allObjections.title: §4.6 RLS policies share mutable predicate
allObjections.detail: All three org-scoped policies duplicate the identical `exists (select 1 from products p where p.id = product_ssot.product_id and p.org_id = ...)` subquery; any future change to the products RLS or JWT claim shape requires coordinated edits across four policies with no single source of truth or test macro.

allObjections.title: §7.1 re-assessment cost bound unenforced
allObjections.detail: The $0.30–$2.00 per-cycle estimate and $15/run ceiling are stated as design assumptions but no mechanism (token counter, Browserless quota guard, or §10 Self-Protect integration) is wired to actually cap or reject runs that would exceed them once Agent #21 Aggressive Crawl is active.

ratification.headline: §9 Q4 lacks clear Panel majority — append-only-vs-UPDATE-with-revision unresolved.

conditions.topic: ProductSSOT §9 Q4 — override semantics. Option Y (append-only, current §3 + §13.1): every mutation appends a NEW override entry; "revoke" = new entry with replacementContent. Option N (UPDATE-with-revision): each override is a top-level entry with a `revisions[]` sub-array; "revoke" = append to that array, current state = LAST revision. Which semantics is canonical for ProductSSOT override mutation?

adversarial.precedent: Kubernetes ConfigMap revision history faced similar unbounded-growth issues with append-only changes, leading to the introduction of revisionHistoryLimit to prevent resource exhaustion.

perReviewer.rejection_steelman: This spec introduces a single point of failure (ProductSSOT write) that can halt all pipeline runs, while providing no operational tooling for the inevitable issues: pruning unbounded arrays, repairing hash chain divergence, or handling write contention. The implementation should be deferred until these operational concerns are addressed with concrete limits, archival strategies, and failure recovery paths.

objections.title: §3.2 saga omits external failure compensation
objections.detail: The three-stage saga table in §3.2 defines compensating actions only for Postgres txn failure (mark unverified) but provides no handler for Vercel deploy succeeding while delta report file write fails; this leaves the run in a half-cleared state where ClearanceRecord Step 6 can still pass despite missing §7 item #3 source disclosure.

objections.title: §4.6 RLS policies share mutable predicate
objections.detail: All three org-scoped policies duplicate the identical `exists (select 1 from products p where p.id = product_ssot.product_id and p.org_id = ...)` subquery; any future change to the products RLS or JWT claim shape requires coordinated edits across four policies with no single source of truth or test macro.

objections.title: §7.1 re-assessment cost bound unenforced
objections.detail: The $0.30–$2.00 per-cycle estimate and $15/run ceiling are stated as design assumptions but no mechanism (token counter, Browserless quota guard, or §10 Self-Protect integration) is wired to actually cap or reject runs that would exceed them once Agent #21 Aggressive Crawl is active.

adversarial.worse_than_status_quo: Making SSOT_WRITE_FAILED visible will convert today's silent bypasses into frequent ERROR verdicts on every transient Postgres blip or hash-chain mismatch, causing more pipeline runs to be marked INCOMPLETE and requiring manual re-trigger than the current zero-visibility status quo.

perReviewer.rejection_steelman: The six-block jsonb-plus-saga design adds substantial operational surface (hash-chain verification, version monotonicity under concurrency, four-way RLS duplication) while the only concrete benefit cited is preserving §7.5 living-document semantics that could be achieved with a simpler append-only event log table; until the open Q4 override semantics and the missing cost-guard implementation are resolved, the spec risks locking in an over-engineered substrate that later waves must carry.

PS-Q4.pick_text: REJECT — none of the listed options is acceptable as specified
PS-Q4.rationale: All four listed shapes either overload the overrides[] array or require UPDATE-in-place; none addresses the need for a first-class revocation entry type that can be independently RLS-gated and cross-referenced from delta_log without polluting the primary override history.

perReviewer.overallNotes: Objections focus exclusively on §3, §4 and §7 surfaces named in the proposal text.

questions.topic: ProductSSOT §9 Q4 — override semantics. Option Y (append-only, current §3 + §13.1): every mutation appends a NEW override entry; "revoke" = new entry with replacementContent. Option N (UPDATE-with-revision): each override is a top-level entry with a `revisions[]` sub-array; "revoke" = append to that array, current state = LAST revision. Which semantics is canonical for ProductSSOT override mutation?

options.text: Y / Append-only — every mutation is a new row; revoke = new override entry with replacementContent. Simpler audit (every change → new product_ssot_version row), matches §28.3's "audit trail preserved" verbatim; cleanest RLS WITH CHECK semantics.

N / UPDATE-with-revision — each override is one top-level entry with revisions[] sub-array; revoke = append to revisions[]. Friendlier UI (single revision-history pane per override), avoids duplicate-key sprawl in the overrides[] jsonb.

Hybrid — db layer stays append-only (product_ssot_version preserves every mutation as a new row), but the `/product-ssot/:productId` UI synthesises an UPDATE-with-revision VIEW from the append-only log. DB is the audit truth, UI is the operator ergonomics.

Different shape entirely — revoke is its own first-class operation (e.g. an `overrideRevocations[]` jsonb that points at active overrides by id), not a synthetic "new override that restores the original". Avoids overloading the override entry with two semantics.
